trial_name: COCA — Calcium for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (2021)
citation: Vallentin MF, Granfeldt A, Meilandt C, Povlsen AL, Sindberg B, Holmberg MJ, et al. Effect of intravenous or intraosseous calcium vs saline on return of spontaneous circulation in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2021;326(22):2268-2276.
one_liner: In adult OHCA, routine calcium chloride did not improve sustained ROSC and showed numerically worse survival, leading to early trial termination for potential harm.

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years) with non-traumatic OHCA receiving CPR by EMS and at least one dose of adrenaline.
pico.intervention: Calcium chloride 5 mmol IV/IO after first adrenaline, repeated after second adrenaline (max 10 mmol).
pico.comparison: Saline placebo IV/IO on same schedule.
pico.outcome: Sustained ROSC (≥20 minutes) (primary); survival and neurological outcomes at 30 days (key secondary).

background.existing_knowledge: Calcium was historically recommended broadly during cardiac arrest, but later restricted to specific indications (hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, calcium-channel blocker toxicity) based on physiological rationale. Observational studies were inconsistent and confounded by resuscitation-time bias. Two small RCTs in 1985 in refractory PEA/asystole showed no clear benefit.
background.knowledge_gap: No modern, adequately powered RCT had tested calcium in the context of contemporary ALS with adrenaline.
background.hypothesis: Calcium administration during OHCA would increase ROSC and improve patient-centred outcomes.

methods.design: Investigator-initiated, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, double-blind, superiority trial.
methods.setting: Prehospital EMS response to OHCA in the Central Denmark Region (multiple ambulance stations; standardised ALS care).

inclusion: Adults (≥18 years) with non-traumatic OHCA receiving CPR by participating EMS and receiving at least one dose of adrenaline during the arrest.
exclusion: Adrenaline administered before arrival of prehospital personnel carrying study drug
Clinical indication for calcium during the arrest (e.g., suspected hyperkalaemia/hypocalcaemia/calcium-channel blocker toxicity)

methods.intervention: Calcium chloride 5 mmol (10 mL) IV or IO immediately after the first dose of adrenaline. Second dose of calcium chloride 5 mmol (10 mL) after the second dose of adrenaline (maximum total calcium chloride 10 mmol).
methods.comparison: 0.9% sodium chloride placebo (10 mL) IV or IO following the same schedule. Otherwise identical standard ALS care.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (identical numbered ampoules; clinicians, participants/surrogates, and outcome assessors masked; unblinding only if clinically necessary).
methods.sample_size_power: Planned sample size 674 to detect a 10% absolute increase in ROSC (from 16% to 26%) with 80% power at alpha 0.05. Trial stopped early after 397 randomised.
secondary_outcomes: Survival at 30 days with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3)
Survival at 90 days with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3)
EQ-5D-5L index and VAS at 30 days

headline_bullets: Sustained ROSC was lower with calcium (19% vs 27%; RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.49–1.03, P=0.09).
30-day survival numerically favoured placebo (5.2% vs 9.1%; RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.27–1.18).
Calcium caused marked hypercalcaemia post-ROSC (74% vs 2%), supporting biological plausibility of harm.
Trial stopped early for potential harm, increasing uncertainty.

outcomes_table.note: Adjusted risk difference −7.6% (95% CI −16.0 to 0.8); P=0.09

outcomes_table.outcome: Survival at 30 days with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3) (key secondary)
Survival at 90 days with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3) (tertiary)

outcomes_table.note: Interpretation limited by very small survivor numbers

outcomes_table.outcome: Hypercalcaemia within 24 hours post-ROSC (ionised Ca >1.33 mmol/L)
outcomes_table.note: Among ROSC patients with ionised calcium measurement; mild 12/35 (34%) and moderate 14/35 (40%) vs mild 1/49 (2%) and moderate 0/49 (0%)
Among patients achieving ROSC; small numbers

subgroup_table.subgroup: PEA with wide QRS/ischemic ECG patterns
subgroup_table.note: Imprecise and event-limited; caution in interpretation

safety: Hypercalcaemia within 24 hours post-ROSC: 74% in calcium group vs 2% in placebo (among measured).
Tachyarrhythmia requiring treatment post-ROSC: 22% vs 26% (among ROSC patients).
Dialysis during hospital admission post-ROSC: 19% vs 6% (among ROSC patients).

domains.notes: 1:1 randomisation using permuted blocks stratified by ambulance station; allocation concealed via masked numbered ampoules.
Double-blind, identical ampoules; post-ROSC hypercalcaemia could unblind in-hospital teams but primary outcome prehospital and survival objective.
Modified ITT: 6 post-randomisation exclusions (traumatic arrests) from primary analysis; small number but potential bias.
Two doses administered in 73% calcium vs 74% placebo; protocol deviations 5% in both; calcium outside protocol 2% vs 1%.
Well balanced: age, sex, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, rhythm distribution similar; adrenaline doses slightly higher in calcium group (median 3 vs 2).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate internal validity: robust design and conduct, but early stopping and modified ITT introduce uncertainty.

domains.notes: Typical adult OHCA demographics; high bystander CPR rate (78%) may not reflect all systems.
Feasible in most ALS systems; exclusions limit applicability to patients with clear calcium indications. Post-resuscitation care variability may affect long-term outcomes.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate external validity: applicable to routine undifferentiated OHCA, but not to cases with specific calcium indications or very different EMS contexts.

strengths: Double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT in prehospital setting.
Objective primary endpoint (sustained ROSC) and registry-based survival follow-up with no loss to follow-up.
Clear pharmacodynamic separation (post-ROSC ionised calcium and hypercalcaemia).
Pragmatic integration into standard ALS workflows.
limitations: Stopped early for potential harm, resulting in underpowered patient-centred outcomes with wide confidence intervals.
Modified ITT analysis with post-randomisation exclusions.
Very small survivor numbers limit neurological and quality-of-life outcome interpretation.
Restriction away from cases with clear calcium indication limits inference to routine empiric use.

critical_appraisal.summary: COCA is a well-conducted double-blind RCT that provides moderate-certainty evidence that routine calcium during undifferentiated OHCA does not improve ROSC and may cause harm. Early stopping and modified ITT reduce confidence, but the consistent direction of effect across outcomes and clear biological mechanism support a recommendation against routine use.

sections.authors_conclusion: Routine calcium chloride during adult OHCA did not improve sustained ROSC and showed numerically worse survival and neurological outcomes; calcium should be restricted to specific clinical indications.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not use routine calcium in undifferentiated adult OHCA; reserve for specific indications (hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, calcium-channel blocker toxicity).
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult non-traumatic OHCA patients without a clear indication for calcium.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Calcium is harmful in all cardiac arrest scenarios; it may still be indicated in specific circumstances.
implementation_caveats: Ensure EMS protocols remove routine calcium administration.
Educate providers on specific indications for calcium.
Monitor for hypercalcaemia if calcium is given for specific indications.

controversies.notes: Trial stopped early after IDMC recommendation for potential harm without formal stopping boundary; improves safety but increases uncertainty and may exaggerate harm magnitude.
Excluding 6 patients with traumatic arrests from primary analysis introduces potential bias, though small.

controversies.topic: Subgroup signal in PEA with wide QRS/ischemic ECG
controversies.notes: ROSC higher with calcium in this subgroup (21% vs 3%), but imprecise and event-limited; caution in interpretation.
Post hoc analysis of longer-term outcomes consistent with index trial directionality, but small numbers.
Post-COCA syntheses conclude no high-certainty evidence of benefit for routine calcium; possible harm.
Contemporary guidelines recommend against routine calcium, aligning with COCA.

context_related_trials.relation: Earlier small trials that did not demonstrate clear survival benefit; COCA provides modern evidence in broader OHCA population.

unresolved_questions: Whether calcium is beneficial in specific subgroups (e.g., PEA with wide QRS/ischemic ECG) remains uncertain.
The mechanism of harm (e.g., reperfusion injury, hypercalcaemia-induced vasospasm) needs further study.
Optimal calcium dosing in true hyperkalaemic arrest is not addressed by COCA.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Routine calcium during adult OHCA does not improve ROSC and may cause harm; restrict to specific indications.
